claim: Animal development is mediated by a surprisingly small set of canonical signaling pathways such as Wnt, Hedgehog, TGF-beta, Notch, and Hippo pathways.
source: Animal development is mediated by a surprisingly small set of canonical signaling pathways such as Wnt, Hedgehog, TGF-beta, Notch, and Hippo pathways.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about animal developmental pathways.

claim: Components of canonical signaling pathways once thought to be present only in animals have been revealed in the closest unicellular relatives of animals by recent genome sequencing.
source: Although once thought to be present only in animals, recent genome sequencing has revealed components of these pathways in the closest unicellular relatives of animals.
evidence: This refers to findings from comparative genomic studies.

claim: Capsaspora owczarzaki is a close unicellular relative of animals that displays aggregative multicellularity.
source: Here, we provide the first functional characterization of any of these developmental pathways in unicellular organisms by developing techniques for genetic manipulation in Capsaspora owczarzaki, a close unicellular relative of animals that displays aggregative multicellularity.
evidence: This is a characterization of the organism used in the study, supported by established knowledge and the manuscript's own observations.

claim: coYki is dispensable for cell proliferation in Capsaspora owczarzaki.
source: In contrast to what might be expected based on studies in animals, we show that coYki is dispensable for cell proliferation but regulates cytoskeletal dynamics and the three-dimensional (3D) shape of multicellular structures.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no significant difference in proliferation between WT and coYki mutant cells.

claim: coYki regulates cytoskeletal dynamics in Capsaspora owczarzaki.
source: In contrast to what might be expected based on studies in animals, we show that coYki is dispensable for cell proliferation but regulates cytoskeletal dynamics and the three-dimensional (3D) shape of multicellular structures.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations of aberrant cytoskeletal dynamics in coYki mutant cells.

claim: coYki regulates the three-dimensional (3D) shape of multicellular structures in Capsaspora owczarzaki.
source: In contrast to what might be expected based on studies in animals, we show that coYki is dispensable for cell proliferation but regulates cytoskeletal dynamics and the three-dimensional (3D) shape of multicellular structures.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing abnormal aggregate morphology in coYki mutants.

claim: The cytoskeletal abnormalities of individual coYki mutant cells underlie the abnormal 3D shape of coYki mutant aggregates.
source: We further demonstrate that the cytoskeletal abnormalities of individual coYki mutant cells underlie the abnormal 3D shape of coYki mutant aggregates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that blebbistatin treatment rescues both cellular and aggregate phenotypes.

claim: The Hippo pathway has an ancestral role in cytoskeletal dynamics and multicellular morphogenesis predating the origin of animal multicellularity.
source: Taken together, these findings implicate an ancestral role for the Hippo pathway in cytoskeletal dynamics and multicellular morphogenesis predating the origin of animal multicellularity, which was co-opted during evolution to regulate cell proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional characterization of coYki in Capsaspora and its evolutionary position.

claim: The Hippo pathway was co-opted during evolution to regulate cell proliferation.
source: Taken together, these findings implicate an ancestral role for the Hippo pathway in cytoskeletal dynamics and multicellular morphogenesis predating the origin of animal multicellularity, which was co-opted during evolution to regulate cell proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that coYki does not regulate proliferation in Capsaspora but YAP/TAZ/Yorkie does in animals.

claim: The vast morphological diversity observed in animals is generated by developmental programs mediated by a surprisingly small set of conserved signaling pathways.
source: The vast morphological diversity observed in animals is generated by developmental programs mediated by a surprisingly small set of conserved signaling pathways (Pires-daSilva and Sommer, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Many components of developmental signaling pathways are present in the closest unicellular relatives of animals.
source: An exciting and unexpected finding from comparative genomic analysis indicates that many components of these pathways are present in the closest unicellular relatives of animals (King et al., 2003; Ros-Rocher et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative genomic studies.

claim: The Hippo pathway coordinates cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival in animals.
source: One such signaling pathway is the Hippo pathway, which coordinates cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival in animals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Hippo pathway in animals.

claim: The Hippo pathway was initially defined as a tumor suppressor pathway that restricts tissue growth in Drosophila development.
source: Initially defined as a tumor suppressor pathway that restricts tissue growth in Drosophila development, Hippo signaling plays a conserved role in organ size control and regeneration in mammals (Davis and Tapon, 2019; Harvey and Hariharan, 2012; Moya and Halder, 2019; Yu et al., 2015; Zheng and Pan, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on the Hippo pathway.

claim: Hippo signaling plays a conserved role in organ size control and regeneration in mammals.
source: Initially defined as a tumor suppressor pathway that restricts tissue growth in Drosophila development, Hippo signaling plays a conserved role in organ size control and regeneration in mammals (Davis and Tapon, 2019; Harvey and Hariharan, 2012; Moya and Halder, 2019; Yu et al., 2015; Zheng and Pan, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The Hippo pathway comprises a core kinase cascade involving sequential activation of Hippo (MST1/2 in mammals) and Warts (LATS1/2 in mammals), which culminates in the phosphorylation and inactivation of Yorkie (YAP/TAZ in mammals).
source: This pathway comprises a core kinase cascade involving sequential activation of two kinases, Hippo (MST1/2 in mammals) and Warts (LATS1/2 in mammals), which culminates in the phosphorylation and inactivation of the potent growth-stimulatory transcriptional coactivator Yorkie (YAP/TAZ in mammals) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Hippo pathway mechanism, also illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The Hippo pathway core kinase cascade is regulated by diverse upstream inputs, most notably mechanical force, the state of the actin cytoskeleton, and cell–cell or cell–substrate adhesion as part of a mechanotransduction pathway.
source: This core kinase cascade is in turn regulated by diverse upstream inputs, most notably mechanical force, the state of the actin cytoskeleton, and cell–cell or cell–substrate adhesion as part of a mechanotransduction pathway that relays mechanical and architectural cues to gene expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hippo pathway regulation.

claim: The Hippo pathway is required for contact inhibition of proliferation in cultured mammalian cells.
source: Echoing its pervasive function in metazoan growth control, the Hippo pathway is required for contact inhibition of proliferation in cultured mammalian cells, and defective Hippo signaling leading to YAP/TAZ oncogene activation is a major driver of human cancers (Davis and Tapon, 2019; Harvey and Hariharan, 2012; Moya and Halder, 2019; Yu et al., 2015; Zheng and Pan, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Defective Hippo signaling leading to YAP/TAZ oncogene activation is a major driver of human cancers.
source: Echoing its pervasive function in metazoan growth control, the Hippo pathway is required for contact inhibition of proliferation in cultured mammalian cells, and defective Hippo signaling leading to YAP/TAZ oncogene activation is a major driver of human cancers (Davis and Tapon, 2019; Harvey and Hariharan, 2012; Moya and Halder, 2019; Yu et al., 2015; Zheng and Pan, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A core Hippo pathway and many upstream regulators are encoded in the genomes of the closest unicellular relatives of animals such as choanoflagellates and filasterians.
source: However, genome sequencing efforts have revealed that a core Hippo pathway and many upstream regulators are encoded in the genomes of the closest unicellular relatives of animals such as choanoflagellates and filasterians (Figure 1B; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Choanoflagellates are flagellated filter feeders that can form multicellular rosette structures by incomplete cytokinesis.
source: The choanoflagellates are flagellated filter feeders that can form multicellular rosette structures by incomplete cytokinesis (Fairclough et al., 2010), whereas filasterians are amoeboid organisms characterized by actin-rich filopodial projections (Figure 1C and D) and represent the most basal known unicellular organism encoding all core components of the Hippo pathway, including upstream kinases and downstream transcriptional machinery (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Filasterians are amoeboid organisms characterized by actin-rich filopodial projections.
source: The choanoflagellates are flagellated filter feeders that can form multicellular rosette structures by incomplete cytokinesis (Fairclough et al., 2010), whereas filasterians are amoeboid organisms characterized by actin-rich filopodial projections (Figure 1C and D) and represent the most basal known unicellular organism encoding all core components of the Hippo pathway, including upstream kinases and downstream transcriptional machinery (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Filasterians represent the most basal known unicellular organism encoding all core components of the Hippo pathway, including upstream kinases and downstream transcriptional machinery.
source: The choanoflagellates are flagellated filter feeders that can form multicellular rosette structures by incomplete cytokinesis (Fairclough et al., 2010), whereas filasterians are amoeboid organisms characterized by actin-rich filopodial projections (Figure 1C and D) and represent the most basal known unicellular organism encoding all core components of the Hippo pathway, including upstream kinases and downstream transcriptional machinery (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Capsaspora owczarzaki is a filasterean originally isolated as a putative endosymbiont in the freshwater snail Biomphalaria glabrata.
source: Capsaspora owczarzaki is a filasterean originally isolated as a putative endosymbiont in the freshwater snail Biomphalaria glabrata that can attack and kill the parasitic schistosome Schistosoma mansoni (Stibbs et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Capsaspora owczarzaki can attack and kill the parasitic schistosome Schistosoma mansoni.
source: Capsaspora owczarzaki is a filasterean originally isolated as a putative endosymbiont in the freshwater snail Biomphalaria glabrata that can attack and kill the parasitic schistosome Schistosoma mansoni (Stibbs et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Capsaspora can be cultured easily in axenic growth medium containing protein source and serum in adherent or shaking culture.
source: Capsaspora can be cultured easily in axenic growth medium containing protein source and serum in adherent or shaking culture and can be transiently transfected, allowing for the examination of protein localization using fluorescent fusion proteins (Parra-Acero et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and the manuscript's own methods.

claim: Capsaspora can be transiently transfected, allowing for the examination of protein localization using fluorescent fusion proteins.
source: Capsaspora can be cultured easily in axenic growth medium containing protein source and serum in adherent or shaking culture and can be transiently transfected, allowing for the examination of protein localization using fluorescent fusion proteins (Parra-Acero et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and the manuscript's own methods.

claim: Under certain conditions Capsaspora cells can adhere to each other to form multicellular aggregates.
source: Although Capsaspora tends to grow as a unicellular organism in laboratory culture conditions, under certain conditions Capsaspora cells can adhere to each other to form multicellular aggregates (Figure 1E–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2013), suggesting that multicellular behaviors may have been selected in the lineage leading to Capsaspora.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and illustrated in figures.

claim: Multicellular behaviors may have been selected in the lineage leading to Capsaspora.
source: Although Capsaspora tends to grow as a unicellular organism in laboratory culture conditions, under certain conditions Capsaspora cells can adhere to each other to form multicellular aggregates (Figure 1E–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2013), suggesting that multicellular behaviors may have been selected in the lineage leading to Capsaspora.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of aggregative behavior.

claim: A complete core Hippo pathway is present in Capsaspora, including an ortholog of the transcriptional coactivator YAP/TAZ/Yorkie.
source: A complete core Hippo pathway is present in Capsaspora, including an ortholog of the transcriptional coactivator YAP/TAZ/Yorkie.
evidence: This is supported by previous genomic studies.

claim: Protein domain architecture is conserved between Capsaspora Yorkie (coYki) and animal YAP/TAZ/Yorkie proteins, including conservation of tandem WW domains, phosphoregulatory sites, and an N-terminal TEAD-binding domain (TBD).
source: Protein domain architecture is conserved between Capsaspora Yorkie (coYki) and animal YAP/TAZ/Yorkie proteins, including conservation of tandem WW domains, phosphoregulatory sites, and an N-terminal TEAD-binding domain (TBD), which mediates YAP/TAZ/Yorkie interaction with its DNA-binding partner TEAD/Sd (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The TEAD-binding domain (TBD) mediates YAP/TAZ/Yorkie interaction with its DNA-binding partner TEAD/Sd.
source: Protein domain architecture is conserved between Capsaspora Yorkie (coYki) and animal YAP/TAZ/Yorkie proteins, including conservation of tandem WW domains, phosphoregulatory sites, and an N-terminal TEAD-binding domain (TBD), which mediates YAP/TAZ/Yorkie interaction with its DNA-binding partner TEAD/Sd (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Coexpression of coYki and the Capsaspora TEAD/Sd ortholog in Drosophila causes upregulation of Hippo pathway target genes.
source: Coexpression of coYki and the Capsaspora TEAD/Sd ortholog in Drosophila causes upregulation of Hippo pathway target genes (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2012), consistent with a role for coYki as a transcriptional regulator as in animals.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: When expressed heterologously in Drosophila S2R+ cells, the Capsaspora Hippo kinase ortholog can induce phosphorylation of coYki.
source: When expressed heterologously in Drosophila S2R+ cells, the Capsaspora Hippo kinase ortholog can induce phosphorylation of coYki (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2012), indicating that a functional Hippo signaling pathway that regulates YAP/TAZ/Yorkie by phosphorylation may have evolved well before the emergence of Metazoa.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A functional Hippo signaling pathway that regulates YAP/TAZ/Yorkie by phosphorylation may have evolved well before the emergence of Metazoa.
source: When expressed heterologously in Drosophila S2R+ cells, the Capsaspora Hippo kinase ortholog can induce phosphorylation of coYki (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2012), indicating that a functional Hippo signaling pathway that regulates YAP/TAZ/Yorkie by phosphorylation may have evolved well before the emergence of Metazoa.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Capsaspora Hippo kinase can phosphorylate coYki.

claim: The Capsaspora genome encodes homologs of other key regulators of animal development such as components of the integrin adhesome.
source: The Capsaspora genome also encodes homologs of other key regulators of animal development such as components of the integrin adhesome (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2010), cadherins (Nichols et al., 2012), tyrosine kinases such as Src and Abl (Suga et al., 2012), NF-kB (Williams and Gilmore, 2020), and p53 (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genomic studies.

claim: The Capsaspora genome encodes homologs of cadherins.
source: The Capsaspora genome also encodes homologs of other key regulators of animal development such as components of the integrin adhesome (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2010), cadherins (Nichols et al., 2012), tyrosine kinases such as Src and Abl (Suga et al., 2012), NF-kB (Williams and Gilmore, 2020), and p53 (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Capsaspora genome encodes homologs of tyrosine kinases such as Src and Abl.
source: The Capsaspora genome also encodes homologs of other key regulators of animal development such as components of the integrin adhesome (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2010), cadherins (Nichols et al., 2012), tyrosine kinases such as Src and Abl (Suga et al., 2012), NF-kB (Williams and Gilmore, 2020), and p53 (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Capsaspora genome encodes homologs of NF-kB.
source: The Capsaspora genome also encodes homologs of other key regulators of animal development such as components of the integrin adhesome (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2010), cadherins (Nichols et al., 2012), tyrosine kinases such as Src and Abl (Suga et al., 2012), NF-kB (Williams and Gilmore, 2020), and p53 (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Capsaspora genome encodes homologs of p53.
source: The Capsaspora genome also encodes homologs of other key regulators of animal development such as components of the integrin adhesome (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2010), cadherins (Nichols et al., 2012), tyrosine kinases such as Src and Abl (Suga et al., 2012), NF-kB (Williams and Gilmore, 2020), and p53 (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Stable Capsaspora cell lines expressing multiple transgenes can be generated.
source: These results demonstrate that stable Capsaspora cell lines expressing multiple transgenes can be generated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing successful generation of stable cell lines with antibiotic resistance markers.

claim: A homozygous coYki disruption mutant was generated in Capsaspora.
source: These results demonstrate the generation of a homozygous coYki disruption mutant (subsequently coYki -/-) and establish a method for the generation of mutants by gene targeting in Capsaspora.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including PCR and sequencing confirmation.

claim: A method for the generation of mutants by gene targeting in Capsaspora has been established.
source: These results demonstrate the generation of a homozygous coYki disruption mutant (subsequently coYki -/-) and establish a method for the generation of mutants by gene targeting in Capsaspora.
evidence: This is supported by the successful generation of coYki mutants using homologous recombination.

claim: There is no significant difference in cell proliferation between WT and coYki -/- cells in adherent culture.
source: In contrast to what may be expected based on previous studies in animal cells, we observed no significant difference in cell proliferation between WT and coYki -/- cells in either condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no significant difference in cell proliferation between WT and coYki -/- cells in shaking culture.
source: In contrast to what may be expected based on previous studies in animal cells, we observed no significant difference in cell proliferation between WT and coYki -/- cells in either condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with the calcium chelator EGTA results in rapid dissociation of Capsaspora aggregates.
source: Treatment with the calcium chelator EGTA resulted in rapid dissociation of the aggregates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that calcium-dependent cell adhesion mediates aggregate integrity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Calcium-dependent cell adhesion mediates aggregate integrity in Capsaspora.
source: Treatment with the calcium chelator EGTA resulted in rapid dissociation of the aggregates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that calcium-dependent cell adhesion mediates aggregate integrity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that EGTA treatment causes aggregate dissociation.

claim: There is no significant difference in the percent of EdU-positive cells between WT and coYki -/- genotypes within aggregates.
source: We used EdU incorporation to label proliferating cells in aggregates and observed no significant difference in the percent of EdU-positive cells between WT and coYki -/- genotypes (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Distribution of EdU+ cells is homogeneous within Capsaspora aggregates.
source: Unlike clones of cultured mammalian cells that often display increased cell proliferation at the clonal boundary (Fisher and Yeh, 1967), distribution of EdU+ cells was homogeneous within Capsaspora aggregates (Figure 2A), suggesting that a mechanism akin to contact-mediated inhibition of proliferation is absent in Capsaspora.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A mechanism akin to contact-mediated inhibition of proliferation is absent in Capsaspora.
source: Unlike clones of cultured mammalian cells that often display increased cell proliferation at the clonal boundary (Fisher and Yeh, 1967), distribution of EdU+ cells was homogeneous within Capsaspora aggregates (Figure 2A), suggesting that a mechanism akin to contact-mediated inhibition of proliferation is absent in Capsaspora.
evidence: This is inferred from the homogeneous distribution of EdU+ cells in aggregates.

claim: The rate of proliferation of Capsaspora is independent of coYki.
source: Together, these results suggest that the rate of proliferation of Capsaspora is independent of coYki or contact inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of proliferation differences between WT and coYki -/- cells.

claim: The rate of proliferation of Capsaspora is independent of contact inhibition.
source: Together, these results suggest that the rate of proliferation of Capsaspora is independent of coYki or contact inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the homogeneous distribution of proliferating cells in aggregates.

claim: coYki -/- aggregates are asymmetric and less circular than WT aggregates.
source: In contrast, coYki -/- aggregates were asymmetric and less circular than WT aggregates (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: WT and coYki -/- aggregate size is not significantly different.
source: Computational analysis of aggregate morphology and size revealed that WT and coYki -/- aggregate size was not significantly different (Figure 2E), whereas coYki -/- aggregates were significantly less circular than WT aggregates (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: coYki -/- aggregates are significantly less circular than WT aggregates.
source: Computational analysis of aggregate morphology and size revealed that WT and coYki -/- aggregate size was not significantly different (Figure 2E), whereas coYki -/- aggregates were significantly less circular than WT aggregates (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: WT aggregates are thicker perpendicular to the culture surface and more spherical than coYki -/- aggregates.
source: Optical sectioning of aggregates expressing mScarlet showed that WT aggregates were thicker perpendicular to the culture surface and more spherical than coYki -/- aggregates (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: coYki -/- aggregates show significantly less curvature than WT aggregates.
source: coYki -/- aggregates showed significantly less curvature than WT aggregates (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that coYki affects the 3D morphology of aggregates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: coYki affects the 3D morphology of aggregates.
source: coYki -/- aggregates showed significantly less curvature than WT aggregates (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that coYki affects the 3D morphology of aggregates.
evidence: This is inferred from the significant difference in curvature between WT and coYki -/- aggregates.

claim: WT cells accrete into round aggregates that fuse with other aggregates when in close proximity but never undergo fission.
source: Time-lapse microscopy of aggregation over a period of 6 days showed that, whereas WT cells accreted into round aggregates that fused with other aggregates when in close proximity but never underwent fission, coYki -/- aggregates were dynamically asymmetrical, less circular than WT, and sometimes underwent fission (Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Video 1.

claim: coYki -/- aggregates are dynamically asymmetrical, less circular than WT, and sometimes undergo fission.
source: Time-lapse microscopy of aggregation over a period of 6 days showed that, whereas WT cells accreted into round aggregates that fused with other aggregates when in close proximity but never underwent fission, coYki -/- aggregates were dynamically asymmetrical, less circular than WT, and sometimes underwent fission (Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Video 1.

claim: coYki plays a critical role in three-dimensional (3D) shape of aggregates.
source: Taken together, these findings uncover a critical role for coYki in three-dimensional (3D) shape of aggregates, but not cell proliferation, in Capsaspora.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple observations of abnormal aggregate morphology in coYki -/- mutants.

claim: coYki does not play a critical role in cell proliferation in Capsaspora.
source: Taken together, these findings uncover a critical role for coYki in three-dimensional (3D) shape of aggregates, but not cell proliferation, in Capsaspora.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of proliferation differences between WT and coYki -/- cells.

claim: The distribution of mCherry-labeled WT or coYki -/- cells within mixed aggregates is similar and no cell sorting is evident.
source: The distribution of mCherry-labeled WT or coYki -/- cells within such mixed aggregates was similar and no cell sorting was evident (Figure 3A–D), indicating that individual coYki -/- cells are competent to adhere to and integrate within aggregates and suggesting that the aberrant morphology of coYki -/- aggregates is an emergent property of a large number of coYki -/- cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A–D.

claim: Individual coYki -/- cells are competent to adhere to and integrate within aggregates.
source: The distribution of mCherry-labeled WT or coYki -/- cells within such mixed aggregates was similar and no cell sorting was evident (Figure 3A–D), indicating that individual coYki -/- cells are competent to adhere to and integrate within aggregates and suggesting that the aberrant morphology of coYki -/- aggregates is an emergent property of a large number of coYki -/- cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of cell sorting in mixed aggregates.

claim: The aberrant morphology of coYki -/- aggregates is an emergent property of a large number of coYki -/- cells.
source: The distribution of mCherry-labeled WT or coYki -/- cells within such mixed aggregates was similar and no cell sorting was evident (Figure 3A–D), indicating that individual coYki -/- cells are competent to adhere to and integrate within aggregates and suggesting that the aberrant morphology of coYki -/- aggregates is an emergent property of a large number of coYki -/- cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that individual coYki -/- cells integrate normally but homogeneous coYki -/- aggregates are abnormal.

claim: The number of cells per cluster is similar for WT and coYki -/- cells after gentle rotation in suspension.
source: The number of cells per cluster was similar for WT and coYki -/- cells (Figure 3E), suggesting that the occurrence of cell–cell adhesion is similar in these genotypes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The occurrence of cell–cell adhesion is similar in WT and coYki -/- genotypes.
source: The number of cells per cluster was similar for WT and coYki -/- cells (Figure 3E), suggesting that the occurrence of cell–cell adhesion is similar in these genotypes.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar number of cells per cluster in WT and coYki -/- cells.

claim: After agitation, significantly more coYki -/- cells remain attached to the substrate compared to WT cells.
source: After agitation, significantly more coYki -/- cells remained attached to the substrate compared to WT cells (Figure 3F), indicating that coYki negatively regulates cell–substrate adhesion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: coYki negatively regulates cell–substrate adhesion.
source: After agitation, significantly more coYki -/- cells remained attached to the substrate compared to WT cells (Figure 3F), indicating that coYki negatively regulates cell–substrate adhesion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that coYki -/- cells show increased substrate adhesion.

claim: Significantly more WT aggregates are nonadherent compared to coYki -/- aggregates.
source: Significantly more WT aggregates were nonadherent compared to coYki -/- aggregates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that coYki negatively regulates aggregate–substrate adhesion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: coYki negatively regulates aggregate–substrate adhesion.
source: Significantly more WT aggregates were nonadherent compared to coYki -/- aggregates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that coYki negatively regulates aggregate–substrate adhesion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that more WT aggregates are nonadherent than coYki -/- aggregates.

claim: coYki affects the morphology of cell aggregates by affecting cell–substrate adhesion but not cell–cell adhesion.
source: Together, our data suggest that coYki affects the morphology of cell aggregates by affecting cell–substrate adhesion but not cell–cell adhesion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations that coYki affects substrate adhesion but not cell-cell adhesion.

claim: The cortices of coYki -/- cells are much more dynamic than those of WT cells.
source: Interestingly, the cortices of coYki -/- cells were much more dynamic than those of WT cells.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy observations.

claim: coYki -/- cells display extensive membrane protrusions and retractions, whereas such dynamic membrane structures are rarely observed in WT cells.
source: Whereas coYki -/- cells display extensive membrane protrusions and retractions, such dynamic membrane structures were rarely observed in WT cells (Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Video 2.

claim: coYki -/- cells show an average of 3.1 protrusions per minute.
source: WT cells rarely showed protrusions. In contrast, coYki -/- cells showed an average of 3.1 protrusions per minute (Figure 4A), a phenotype that was rescued in coYki -/- cells expressing a coYki transgene (Figure 4A, Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The protrusion phenotype of coYki -/- cells is rescued by expression of a coYki transgene.
source: WT cells rarely showed protrusions. In contrast, coYki -/- cells showed an average of 3.1 protrusions per minute (Figure 4A), a phenotype that was rescued in coYki -/- cells expressing a coYki transgene (Figure 4A, Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Video 3.

claim: coYki affects the cortical dynamics of Capsaspora cells.
source: These results suggest that coYki affects the cortical dynamics of Capsaspora cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of increased protrusions in coYki -/- cells.

claim: Capsaspora undergoes F-actin-mediated amoeboid locomotion.
source: At the basal side of WT cells, LifeAct-mScarlet was often enriched at the cell edge corresponding to the direction of cell movement, suggesting that Capsaspora undergoes F-actin-mediated amoeboid locomotion (Video 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of LifeAct-mScarlet enrichment at the leading edge of moving cells.

claim: Actin-rich structures mediate cell–substrate interaction in Capsaspora.
source: As cells move, some LifeAct-mScarlet signal appears as stationary foci on the basal surface, suggesting the existence of actin-rich structures that mediate cell–substrate interaction in Capsaspora (Figure 4B, Video 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of stationary LifeAct-mScarlet foci during cell movement.

claim: F-actin is enriched at a circular cell cortex in WT cells.
source: Optical sections at mid-height of WT cells showed that F-actin was enriched at a circular cell cortex, where transient bursts of small F-actin puncta were often observed (Figure 4B, Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Video 5.

claim: Cortical shape is less circular in coYki -/- cells.
source: In contrast, cortical shape was less circular in coYki -/- cells, and F-actin concentration along the cortex was less uniform (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: F-actin concentration along the cortex is less uniform in coYki -/- cells.
source: In contrast, cortical shape was less circular in coYki -/- cells, and F-actin concentration along the cortex was less uniform (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: During the formation of membrane protrusions in coYki -/- cells, F-actin is initially depleted compared to the rest of the cell.
source: During the formation of the membrane protrusions produced by coYki -/- cells, F-actin was initially depleted compared to the rest of the cell (Figure 4C, Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Video 6.

claim: After membrane protrusions in coYki -/- cells have fully extended, F-actin accumulates first at the distal end and then along the entire cortex of the protrusion, followed by regression of the protrusion.
source: After the membrane protrusions had fully extended, F-actin accumulated first at the distal end and then along the entire cortex of the protrusion, followed by the regression of the protrusion.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy observations.

claim: The protrusions observed in coYki -/- cells are actin-depleted blebs.
source: These results suggest that the protrusions observed in coYki -/- cells are actin-depleted blebs, and that after bleb formation, F-actin reaccumulates within the bleb, leading to cortical reformation and bleb regression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that protrusions initially lack F-actin and then accumulate it.

claim: After bleb formation in coYki -/- cells, F-actin reaccumulates within the bleb, leading to cortical reformation and bleb regression.
source: These results suggest that the protrusions observed in coYki -/- cells are actin-depleted blebs, and that after bleb formation, F-actin reaccumulates within the bleb, leading to cortical reformation and bleb regression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed sequence of F-actin dynamics during protrusion formation and regression.

claim: coYki -/- cells within aggregates show dynamic formation of actin-depleted blebs.
source: As in adherent cells, coYki -/- cells within aggregates showed dynamic formation of actin-depleted blebs (Video 7).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Video 7.

claim: coYki -/- cells show aberrant cortical cytoskeleton and excessive membrane blebbing in both isolated adherent cells and within aggregates.
source: Thus, coYki -/- cells show aberrant cortical cytoskeleton and excessive membrane blebbing in both isolated adherent cells and within aggregates.
evidence: This is inferred from observations in both adherent culture and aggregates.

claim: The cellular phenotypes observed in coYki -/- cells (membrane blebbing and related cortical cytoskeletal defects) may underlie the aberrant aggregate morphology.
source: Loss of coYki causes both bleb-like protrusions and abnormal aggregate morphology, suggesting that the cellular phenotypes observed in coYki -/- cells (membrane blebbing and related cortical cytoskeletal defects) may underlie the aberrant aggregate morphology.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-occurrence of cellular and aggregate phenotypes.

claim: Low concentrations of blebbistatin suppress the formation of blebs in coYki -/- cells.
source: Strikingly, not only did low concentrations of blebbistatin suppress the formation of blebs in coYki -/- cells (Figure 4D, Video 8), blebbistatin also rescued the abnormal morphology of coYki -/- aggregates (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Video 8.

claim: Blebbistatin rescues the abnormal morphology of coYki -/- aggregates.
source: Strikingly, not only did low concentrations of blebbistatin suppress the formation of blebs in coYki -/- cells (Figure 4D, Video 8), blebbistatin also rescued the abnormal morphology of coYki -/- aggregates (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: coYki -/- aggregates treated with blebbistatin are circular and resemble WT aggregates.
source: Whereas coYki -/- cell aggregates were asymmetric and showed low circularity (Figure 4E'''), coYki -/- aggregates treated with blebbistatin were circular and resembled WT aggregates (Figure 4E'''' and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: There is a causal link between the membrane/cytoskeletal defects observed in individual coYki -/- cells and the abnormal morphology of coYki -/- aggregates.
source: These results suggest a causal link between the membrane/cytoskeletal defects observed in individual coYki -/- cells and the abnormal morphology of coYki -/- aggregates.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blebbistatin rescues both cellular and aggregate phenotypes.

claim: In mammals and in Drosophila, YAP/TAZ/Yorkie is regulated by cytoplasmic sequestration in response to phosphorylation of HXRXXS motifs by the LATS/Warts kinases.
source: In mammals and in Drosophila, YAP/TAZ/Yorkie is regulated by cytoplasmic sequestration in response to phosphorylation of HXRXXS motifs by the LATS/Warts kinases (Zheng and Pan, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: coYki has three HXRXXS motifs that align with HXRXXS motifs on YAP and an additional nonconserved N-terminal HXRXXS motif.
source: coYki has three HXRXXS motifs that align with HXRXXS motifs on YAP and an additional nonconserved N-terminal HXRXXS motif (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cells transfected with mScarlet-coYki show mScarlet enriched in the cytoplasm relative to the nucleus.
source: Cells transfected with mScarlet-coYki showed mScarlet enriched in the cytoplasm relative to the nucleus (Figure 5B and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and E.

claim: The majority of cells transfected with mScarlet-coYki 4SA show uniform mScarlet signal throughout the cell or enriched mScarlet signal in the nucleus.
source: In contrast, the majority of cells transfected with mScarlet-coYki 4SA showed uniform mScarlet signal throughout the cell or enriched mScarlet signal in the nucleus (Figure 5C and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and F.

claim: mScarlet fluorescence is reduced in the nucleus relative to the cytoplasm in cells expressing mScarlet-coYki.
source: Whereas mScarlet fluorescence was reduced in the nucleus relative to the cytoplasm in cells expressing mScarlet-coYki (Figure 5G), fluorescence intensity was similar in the nucleus and cytoplasm in cells expressing mScarlet-coYki 4SA (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Fluorescence intensity is similar in the nucleus and cytoplasm in cells expressing mScarlet-coYki 4SA.
source: Whereas mScarlet fluorescence was reduced in the nucleus relative to the cytoplasm in cells expressing mScarlet-coYki (Figure 5G), fluorescence intensity was similar in the nucleus and cytoplasm in cells expressing mScarlet-coYki 4SA (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: HXRXXS motifs affect the subcellular localization of coYki.
source: These results show that HXRXXS motifs affect the subcellular localization of coYki and suggest that, like in animals, phosphorylation of coYki by Hippo signaling leads to cytoplasmic sequestration.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential localization of wild-type and mutant coYki.

claim: Like in animals, phosphorylation of coYki by Hippo signaling leads to cytoplasmic sequestration.
source: These results show that HXRXXS motifs affect the subcellular localization of coYki and suggest that, like in animals, phosphorylation of coYki by Hippo signaling leads to cytoplasmic sequestration.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutation of phosphorylation sites affects coYki localization.

claim: The function of coYki as a transcriptional regulator and Hippo pathway effector is conserved between Capsaspora and animals.
source: This regulation of coYki nuclear localization, along with the previous finding that coYki can induce the expression of Hippo pathway genes when expressed in Drosophila (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2012), suggests that the function of coYki as a transcriptional regulator and Hippo pathway effector is conserved between Capsaspora and animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of phosphorylation-dependent localization and previous functional studies.

claim: RNA-seq analysis revealed 1205 differentially expressed genes in coYki -/- cells, including 397 downregulated and 808 upregulated genes.
source: This analysis revealed 1205 differentially expressed genes, including 397 downregulated (Supplementary file 1) and 808 upregulated genes (Supplementary file 2) in the coYki mutant.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Genes predicted to encode actin-binding proteins are enriched in the set of genes upregulated in the coYki -/- mutant.
source: Genes predicted to encode actin-binding proteins were enriched in the set of genes upregulated in the coYki -/- mutant (Supplementary file 3), suggesting that these genes may play a role in the aberrant cytoskeletal dynamics observed in coYki -/- cells.
evidence: This is supported by functional enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Genes upregulated in coYki -/- cells may play a role in the aberrant cytoskeletal dynamics observed in coYki -/- cells.
source: Genes predicted to encode actin-binding proteins were enriched in the set of genes upregulated in the coYki -/- mutant (Supplementary file 3), suggesting that these genes may play a role in the aberrant cytoskeletal dynamics observed in coYki -/- cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of actin-binding protein genes in upregulated genes.

claim: coYki may regulate cytoskeletal dynamics in a transcription-independent manner.
source: Nevertheless, we cannot formally exclude the possibility that coYki may also regulate cytoskeletal dynamics in a transcription-independent manner, an example of which has been reported in Drosophila (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation based on previous findings in Drosophila.

claim: Cell movement and cell migration are the two most significantly enriched functional categories among mammalian orthologs of genes differentially expressed in coYki -/- cells.
source: Ingenuity Pathway Analysis of this mammalian ortholog set showed that the two most significantly enriched functional categories corresponded to cell movement and cell migration (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Regulation of cell migration was reported as the most enriched functional category among YAP target genes in glioblastoma cells.
source: Notably, regulation of cell migration was reported as the most enriched functional category among YAP target genes in glioblastoma cells (Stein et al., 2015), and cell motility was an enriched category in an integrative analysis of gene regulatory networks downstream of YAP/TAZ utilizing transcriptomic and cistromic data from multiple human tissues (Paczkowska et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cell motility was an enriched category in an integrative analysis of gene regulatory networks downstream of YAP/TAZ utilizing transcriptomic and cistromic data from multiple human tissues.
source: Notably, regulation of cell migration was reported as the most enriched functional category among YAP target genes in glioblastoma cells (Stein et al., 2015), and cell motility was an enriched category in an integrative analysis of gene regulatory networks downstream of YAP/TAZ utilizing transcriptomic and cistromic data from multiple human tissues (Paczkowska et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: No enrichment was detected in functional categories of cell proliferation or the cell cycle among mammalian orthologs of genes differentially expressed in coYki -/- cells.
source: However, in contrast to functional enrichment studies in metazoan systems examining genes regulated by YAP/TAZ/Yorkie (Ikmi et al., 2014; Stein et al., 2015; Zanconato et al., 2015), no enrichment was detected in functional categories of cell proliferation or the cell cycle (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The lack of enrichment in cell proliferation or cell cycle categories is consistent with the lack of a proliferative phenotype in coYki -/- cells.
source: This finding is consistent with the lack of a proliferative phenotype in coYki -/- cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between transcriptomic and phenotypic data.

claim: coYki regulates cytoskeletal dynamics at the cell cortex.
source: By developing tools for genome editing in Capsaspora, we demonstrate that coYki regulates cytoskeletal dynamics at the cell cortex but is dispensable for the proliferation of Capsaspora cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations of cytoskeletal defects in coYki -/- cells.

claim: coYki-dependent cortical cytoskeletal function regulates the 3D shape of Capsaspora aggregates in a manner that may involve tuning the strength of cell–substrate adhesion.
source: Such coYki-dependent cortical cytoskeletal function, in turn, regulates the 3D shape of Capsaspora aggregates in a manner that may involve tuning the strength of cell–substrate adhesion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations of both cytoskeletal and adhesion phenotypes in coYki -/- cells.

claim: Cytoskeletal regulation is an ancestral function of YAP/TAZ/Yorkie predating the origin of Metazoa.
source: Our findings implicate cytoskeletal regulation as an ancestral function of YAP/TAZ/Yorkie predating the origin of Metazoa and suggest that this gene acquired the function of cell proliferation control after the last common ancestor of Capsaspora and animals in the lineage leading to animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional characterization of coYki in Capsaspora.

claim: YAP/TAZ/Yorkie acquired the function of cell proliferation control after the last common ancestor of Capsaspora and animals in the lineage leading to animals.
source: Our findings implicate cytoskeletal regulation as an ancestral function of YAP/TAZ/Yorkie predating the origin of Metazoa and suggest that this gene acquired the function of cell proliferation control after the last common ancestor of Capsaspora and animals in the lineage leading to animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that coYki does not regulate proliferation but animal YAP/TAZ/Yorkie does.

claim: In early-diverging ctenophores and cnidarians, Hippo pathway activity is enriched in proliferating tissues.
source: This co-option likely occurred early in the animal lineage, as in early-diverging ctenophores and cnidarians Hippo pathway activity is enriched in proliferating tissues (Coste et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The co-option of YAP/TAZ/Yorkie for cell proliferation control in early metazoans may have provided a convenient mechanism that couples cell proliferation with cytoskeletal and mechanical properties of cells.
source: Given that the cortical cytoskeleton is both an important upstream regulator and a downstream effector of Hippo signaling in animal cells (Deng et al., 2020; Fernández et al., 2011; Gaspar and Tapon, 2014; Sun and Irvine, 2016), the co-option of YAP/TAZ/Yorkie for cell proliferation control in early metazoans may have provided a convenient mechanism that couples cell proliferation with cytoskeletal and mechanical properties of cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known relationships between cytoskeleton and Hippo signaling.

claim: The abnormal 3D shape of coYki -/- aggregates is due to increased cell–substrate adhesion without affecting cell–cell adhesion.
source: Our study suggests that the abnormal 3D shape of coYki -/- aggregates is due to increased cell–substrate adhesion without affecting cell–cell adhesion.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations of adhesion properties.

claim: Capsaspora encodes an integrin adhesome.
source: Capsaspora encodes an integrin adhesome (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2010), and Capsaspora cell–substrate adhesion is mediated at least in part by integrins (Parra-Acero et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Capsaspora cell–substrate adhesion is mediated at least in part by integrins.
source: Capsaspora encodes an integrin adhesome (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2010), and Capsaspora cell–substrate adhesion is mediated at least in part by integrins (Parra-Acero et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Two integrin-β genes (CAOG_05058 and CAOG_01283) are upregulated in coYki -/- cells.
source: Indeed, our RNA-seq data shows that two integrin-β genes (CAOG_05058 and CAOG_01283) are upregulated in coYki -/- cells, suggesting a potential contribution by integrins in this phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Integrins may contribute to the increased cell-substrate adhesion phenotype in coYki -/- cells.
source: Indeed, our RNA-seq data shows that two integrin-β genes (CAOG_05058 and CAOG_01283) are upregulated in coYki -/- cells, suggesting a potential contribution by integrins in this phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the upregulation of integrin genes in coYki -/- cells.

claim: The strength of integrin-mediated focal adhesions can be regulated by cytoskeletal contractility.
source: Given that the strength of integrin-mediated focal adhesions can be regulated by cytoskeletal contractility (Dumbauld et al., 2010), the aberrant cytoskeletal properties of coYki -/- cells may also contribute to their abnormal cell–substrate adhesion.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The aberrant cytoskeletal properties of coYki -/- cells may contribute to their abnormal cell–substrate adhesion.
source: Given that the strength of integrin-mediated focal adhesions can be regulated by cytoskeletal contractility (Dumbauld et al., 2010), the aberrant cytoskeletal properties of coYki -/- cells may also contribute to their abnormal cell–substrate adhesion.
evidence: This is inferred from the known relationship between cytoskeleton and adhesion.

claim: Blebbistatin can rescue the aberrant morphology of coYki -/- aggregates, which is consistent with the possibility that cytoskeletal contractility contributes to the adhesion phenotype.
source: This possibility is consistent with our data showing that blebbistatin, which inhibits myosin and thus perturbs cytoskeletal contractility, can rescue the aberrant morphology of coYki -/- aggregates.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of aggregate morphology by blebbistatin.

claim: The emergence of multicellularity is driven by phagotrophic predators of unicellular organisms as multicellular aggregates are less likely to be consumed by phagotrophic predators and thus are selectively favored.
source: It has been suggested that the emergence of multicellularity is driven by phagotrophic predators of unicellular organisms as multicellular aggregates are less likely to be consumed by phagotrophic predators and thus are selectively favored (Stanley, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A round aggregate shape ensures maximum contact between cells within the group, reducing the chance of a cell disassociating and thus being vulnerable to predation.
source: A round aggregate shape ensures maximum contact between cells within the group, reducing the chance of a cell disassociating and thus being vulnerable to predation.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the benefits of round aggregate shape.

claim: By increasing the roundness of aggregates, coYki could potentially affect sedimentation rate.
source: By increasing the roundness of aggregates, coYki could potentially affect either of these phenotypes: the shape of particles affects sedimentation rate (Yokojima et al., 2021), and a more round shape minimizes surface area, thus potentially resulting in more interior cells that are shielded from stress.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known relationship between shape and sedimentation.

claim: A more round shape minimizes surface area, thus potentially resulting in more interior cells that are shielded from stress.
source: By increasing the roundness of aggregates, coYki could potentially affect either of these phenotypes: the shape of particles affects sedimentation rate (Yokojima et al., 2021), and a more round shape minimizes surface area, thus potentially resulting in more interior cells that are shielded from stress.
evidence: This is speculation based on geometric principles.

claim: A YAP loss-of-function mutation in medaka fish causes a tissue flattening phenotype.
source: Interestingly, a YAP loss-of-function mutation in medaka fish causes a tissue flattening phenotype (Porazinski et al., 2015) similar to that observed in coYki -/- Capsaspora aggregates (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and illustrated in Figure 6D.

claim: The regulation of 3D tissue architecture is an ancient and conserved function of YAP/TAZ/Yorkie predating the origin of animal multicellularity.
source: Although we cannot rule out independent acquisition of this Yorkie/YAP function in these two lineages, such phenotypic similarity suggests that the regulation of 3D tissue architecture is an ancient and conserved function of YAP/TAZ/Yorkie predating the origin of animal multicellularity.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic similarity between medaka and Capsaspora.

claim: YAP/TAZ/Yorkie may have first been selected during evolution to regulate the 3D shape of multicellular aggregates in unicellular ancestors of animals.
source: We speculate that YAP/TAZ/Yorkie may have first been selected during evolution to regulate the 3D shape of multicellular aggregates in unicellular ancestors of animals, and evolved later to also control organ size in order to maintain appropriate scaling between the size of an organ and the size of the body as a whole.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary trajectory of YAP/TAZ/Yorkie function.

claim: YAP/TAZ/Yorkie evolved later to control organ size in order to maintain appropriate scaling between the size of an organ and the size of the body as a whole.
source: We speculate that YAP/TAZ/Yorkie may have first been selected during evolution to regulate the 3D shape of multicellular aggregates in unicellular ancestors of animals, and evolved later to also control organ size in order to maintain appropriate scaling between the size of an organ and the size of the body as a whole.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary trajectory of YAP/TAZ/Yorkie function.
